title: The legal & regulatory landscape
blurb: Explain how law and regulation shape a project's working conditions, risk management, governance and sustainability.
question: A housing association is building 40 new homes. The board asks the project manager how the legal and regulatory landscape will affect the project's working conditions, risk management, governance and sustainability. What should she tell them?

teach.h: Every project sits inside the law
teach.body: The legal and regulatory landscape is the set of laws (Acts of Parliament and regulations) and regulators' rules that apply to a project's people, activities and outputs. It is not just a constraint to tick off: it shapes how people work, which risks matter most, what governance is needed and how sustainable the solution must be. In plain English: the law decides some of your project's requirements for you, and they are not up for negotiation.

children.label: Working conditions
children.sub: health and safety, employment, working time, equality

teach.h: UK laws a project manager should recognise
head: Law
What it means for a project
rows: Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974
Protect workers and others, so far as reasonably practicable
Plan and manage health and safety on construction projects
Handle personal data lawfully, fairly and securely
No discrimination; reasonable adjustments for disabled people
Bribes are offences; firms can be liable for failing to prevent them
teach.caption: You are not expected to be a lawyer: recognise which laws apply, and get specialist advice on the detail.

teach.body: Health and safety law requires risk assessments, safe systems of work, training and welfare facilities. On construction projects, the CDM Regulations 2015 name duty holders (such as the client, principal designer and principal contractor) and require a construction phase plan. Employment law sets contracts, pay and working time, including an average 48-hour weekly limit unless a worker opts out, and rest breaks. Equality law requires fair treatment. All of these shape the schedule, resourcing and cost estimates.

steps.label: Identify the law
steps.sub: which laws and regulators apply here?

steps.label: Assess the risk
steps.sub: chance and impact of a breach, incl. penalties

steps.label: Watch for change
steps.sub: new laws reassessed as soon as known

teach.caption: Breaches can mean fines, prosecution, work being stopped, delays and reputational damage. That makes compliance a major source of project risk.

teach.body: Regulation adds GOVERNANCE requirements: approvals, audit trails, reporting duties and records that prove compliance. UK GDPR may require a data protection impact assessment before high-risk processing; anti-bribery controls such as a gifts and hospitality register and supplier due diligence protect the organisation. For SUSTAINABILITY, environmental regulation on waste, emissions and planning consent shapes design choices, materials, suppliers and site practices, and must be reflected in the success criteria.

teach.h: Handling legal requirements: linear vs iterative

rows.label: Capture
values: Up front, in concept and definition
Early, then refined in the backlog

rows.label: Checking
values: In the definition of done, every increment

rows.label: Approval
values: Still needed before each release goes live

teach.text: Exam traps. 1) Legal requirements are never 'nice to haves' to trade away for time or cost. 2) Compliance can't be handed off: accountability doesn't transfer to the sponsor or a regulator. 3) Don't wait for a new law to come into force: assess its impact as soon as it is known. 4) Law affects more than safety: governance and sustainability too.

teach.body: Working conditions: Joanna's client appoints a principal designer and principal contractor under CDM 2015, and night concrete pours are planned within working-time limits. Risk: a new building safety requirement is logged and assessed the week it is announced. Governance: residents' data is handled under UK GDPR, and a supplier's offer of a free holiday is declined and recorded under the anti-bribery policy. Sustainability: planning consent conditions limit site hours and require drainage and waste controls.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Working conditions: name a law (e.g. HASAWA 1974, CDM 2015, working time) and its effect on the team.
Risk management: compliance as a risk, penalties for breach, controls and monitoring.
Governance: extra approvals, audits and reporting duties (e.g. UK GDPR, Bribery Act 2010).
Sustainability: environmental rules on waste, emissions and planning shape design and suppliers.
Close with the consequence: fines, stoppage, delay, reputation, so seek specialist advice early.
The legal and regulatory landscape shapes working conditions, risk management, governance and sustainability.
Key UK examples: HASAWA 1974, CDM 2015, Data Protection Act 2018 / UK GDPR, Equality Act 2010, Bribery Act 2010.
Non-compliance risks fines, prosecution, stopped work, delay and reputational damage.
Legal requirements are non-negotiable: fixed scope in linear, 'Must have' in iterative.
Assess new or changing laws as soon as they are known and get specialist advice.

summary: You can now explain how the legal and regulatory landscape affects a project's working conditions, risk management, governance and sustainability, using real UK laws as examples. You can also explain why legal requirements are non-negotiable and how they are handled in linear and iterative life cycles.

A.q: Which aspect of a project is most directly affected by the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974?
A.why: The Act places duties on employers to protect the health, safety and welfare of workers and others, which directly shapes working conditions.

whyNot.0: Benefits realisation is about achieving the business case benefits, not safety duties.
whyNot.2: Brand identity is not what health and safety law governs.
whyNot.3: Safety requirements are not open to prioritising away; the Act's main impact is on how people work.

A.q: Which law governs how a UK project handles personal data?
options: Health and Safety at Work etc. Act
UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018
A.why: Personal data in the UK is governed by UK GDPR together with the Data Protection Act 2018.

whyNot.0: This Act covers health, safety and welfare at work.
whyNot.1: CDM covers construction health and safety; the Equality Act covers discrimination.
whyNot.3: The Bribery Act covers bribery offences, and company law is not the data protection regime.

A.q: The CDM Regulations 2015 apply mainly to which kind of project?
A.why: The Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015 manage health and safety on construction projects.

whyNot.0: Software projects are not construction work, so CDM doesn't apply to them.
whyNot.1: Marketing campaigns are not construction work.
whyNot.2: Financial audits are not construction work.

B.q: A new regulation adds reporting duties to a project already under way. What is the most likely impact on governance?
options: More approvals, records and audit evidence
Fewer stakeholders need to be informed
The business case no longer needs review
The PM's delegated authority is increased
B.why: Regulation typically adds governance requirements: approvals, records and evidence that the project complies.

whyNot.1: New reporting duties usually widen, not narrow, who must be informed.
whyNot.2: A regulatory change is a reason to review the business case, not to stop reviewing it.
whyNot.3: Extra regulation tends to tighten control rather than increase delegated authority.

B.q: A supplier bidding for a project contract offers the project manager an expensive holiday. Which law is most relevant?
B.why: Offering or accepting an advantage to influence a contract decision may be bribery under the Bribery Act 2010. The PM should decline and record it under the organisation's policy.

whyNot.0: The Equality Act covers discrimination, not inducements.
whyNot.1: Data protection law covers personal data.
whyNot.3: Working time rules cover hours, breaks and leave.

B.q: How can the legal landscape affect a project's sustainability?
options: Rules on waste and emissions shape design
It only applies after the project closes
It removes the need for sustainability KPIs
B.why: Environmental regulation on waste, emissions and planning consent shapes design, materials, suppliers and site practices.

whyNot.0: Law affects governance, risk and sustainability, not only safety.
whyNot.2: Environmental rules apply during delivery as well as afterwards.
whyNot.3: Compliance is evidenced through measures, so KPIs are still needed.

C.q: A change in the law affecting the project has been announced and will come into force in six months, before handover. What should the project manager do first?
options: Wait until it is in force before acting
Ask the regulator for a project exemption
Leave it to operations after handover
Assess its impact on the project now
C.why: A known change should be assessed straight away and then managed through the risk, issue and change processes, so the project can comply on time.

whyNot.0: Waiting leaves too little time to respond and risks non-compliance at handover.
whyNot.1: Exemptions are not a normal response; the project should plan to comply.
whyNot.2: The law takes effect before handover, so the project must deal with it.

C.q: On an iterative project to build a public sector website, the team learns the site must meet accessibility regulations. How should this requirement be prioritised?
options: As a 'Must have' that can't be traded
As a 'Could have' if there is time
As a 'Won't have' for a later release
As a 'Should have' the PO may defer
C.why: Legal and regulatory requirements are non-negotiable, so they are 'Must haves' in MoSCoW prioritisation.

whyNot.1: A 'Could have' may be dropped, which a legal requirement cannot be.
whyNot.2: Deferring it would mean releasing a non-compliant service.
whyNot.3: A 'Should have' can be deferred; a legal requirement cannot.

C.q:
Which THREE are likely consequences of a project failing to comply with the law?
1. Fines or prosecution
2. Work stopped by a regulator
3. An automatic budget increase
4. Reputational damage
C.why: Non-compliance can bring fines or prosecution, enforcement action that stops work, and reputational damage.

whyNot.0: No automatic budget increase (3) follows a breach; the costs fall on the project.
whyNot.1: Includes a budget increase (3), which is not a consequence, and leaves out fines (1).
whyNot.3: Includes a budget increase (3) and leaves out work being stopped (2).

reteach.title: Running a weekend music festival
reteach.question: Picture organising a two-day music festival in a park. Which rules shape the event, and how do they touch working conditions, risk, governance and sustainability?

blocks.h: The rules shape the whole event
blocks.body: Crew need safe working practices and rest between long shifts (working conditions). Crowd safety and licence conditions are the biggest risks, because a breach could close the event (risk). The licensing authority wants plans approved and records kept (governance). Noise curfews, waste and litter rules and protecting the park shape the site plan (sustainability). The organiser can't negotiate any of these away; they plan around them from day one.

blocks.text: The licence rules aren't a 'nice to have' you drop when budget is tight. Neither are a project's legal requirements.

explain.body: Health and safety law (HASAWA 1974, CDM 2015 on construction), employment law, working time rules and equality law decide how people must be protected and treated. They drive risk assessments, training, rest, welfare and fair treatment.

items.label: Health and Safety at Work etc. Act
average weekly limit unless opted out

test.q: A project plans 12-hour shifts, six days a week, for three months to recover a delay. Which area of law most directly constrains this plan?
test.why: Working time rules limit average weekly hours (unless a worker opts out) and require rest breaks, so they directly constrain this recovery plan.

whyNot.1: Data protection covers personal data, not hours worked.
whyNot.3: Planning law covers land use and development consent, not staff hours.

explain.body: Every applicable law creates a compliance risk. Breaches can bring fines, prosecution, enforcement action that stops work, delay and reputational damage. Identify applicable laws, assess the risks, put controls in place, monitor them and watch for changes.

test.q: Which statement best describes the role of legislation in project risk management?
options: It transfers all risk to the regulator
It sets minimum standards to be met
It applies only once the project closes
It removes the need for a risk register
test.why: Legislation sets minimum standards the project must meet, so failing to meet them is a risk that must be managed.

whyNot.0: Regulators enforce the law; they don't take on the project's risk.
whyNot.2: Legal duties apply throughout the project, not just after closure.
whyNot.3: Compliance risks are recorded and managed like other risks.

explain.body: Laws and regulators add approvals, audits, reporting duties and record-keeping. UK GDPR may require a data protection impact assessment; the Bribery Act 2010 means gifts and hospitality are controlled and recorded.

test.q: A project will start processing customers' health data in a new way that is likely to be high risk. Under UK GDPR, which governance step may be required before processing begins?
test.why: UK GDPR requires a data protection impact assessment (DPIA) before processing that is likely to result in a high risk to individuals.

whyNot.0: A post-implementation review happens after delivery, too late to shape lawful processing.
whyNot.1: A benefits realisation plan tracks benefits, not data protection risks.
whyNot.2: A gifts and hospitality register is an anti-bribery control.

explain.body: Environmental regulation covers waste, emissions, pollution and planning consent. It shapes the options considered, design, materials, suppliers and site practices, and should appear in the project's sustainability objectives and success criteria.

test.q: A new regulation requires a construction project to report the carbon emissions of the materials it uses. Which area of legal and regulatory impact does this mainly illustrate?
test.why: Rules on emissions are environmental regulation, which shapes the project's sustainability choices and reporting.

whyNot.0: Working conditions concern how people are protected and treated at work.
whyNot.2: Team development is about building team capability, not regulatory impact.
whyNot.3: Resource levelling is a scheduling technique, not an area of legal impact.
